stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a 1904 play. Mr. Pell, an amateur bird collector, has just shown his niece Agnes a drawer of mounted warblers.
PELL: There, every one labeled. Thou canst not know a bird till thou hast it in hand.
AGNES: And what hast thou learned of it, Uncle, save the colour of its coat? This one sang at dawn from the alder, I'd wager, and fed its young on midges. If the drawer holds only feathers, then all the bird's life went out of it with its breath. Ere you take another, sit an hour by the marsh and watch.
choices: Agnes argues that a mounted specimen shows how a bird looked but reveals little about how it lived.
Agnes comes to accept that a bird must be collected and labeled before it can be properly studied.
Agnes asks her uncle to explain what the warblers' feathers have taught him about their coloring.
Agnes argues that collecting warblers should be forbidden because it threatens the marsh's birds.
explanation: Put Agnes's lines into plain English: a drawer of skins tells you only the bird's color, while its singing, feeding and raising of young are lost when it dies. Her conditional ('If the drawer holds only feathers, then...') and her advice to watch living birds both make one point: specimens show appearance, not behavior. That claim covers everything she says.

B.why: This is Pell's position, not Agnes's. You matched the other character's line, and Agnes rejects that view instead of accepting it.

C.why: You read 'what hast thou learned of it' as a real question. It is rhetorical: Agnes means he has learned almost nothing, so she is not actually asking for an explanation.

D.why: Agnes asks her uncle to watch before he collects again. She never calls for a ban or says the marsh's birds are under threat, so this choice claims more than the text supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in an English weaving village in 1822. Mr. Cartwell, a mill owner, has told the hand weaver Hannah Doyle that his new power looms will free weavers from their toil.
HANNAH: Free us, sir? Aye, free us of our bread. If your engine weaves in a day what I weave in a week, then who will pay me for the other six days? You call it relief. But a weaver relieved of her loom is only a woman with empty hands and a hungry family.
choices: Hannah argues that power looms will strip hand weavers of their income instead of easing their labor.
Hannah agrees that power looms will spare hand weavers the long hours their work currently demands.
Hannah asks Cartwell to explain how he plans to pay weavers for the days the new looms stand idle.
Hannah argues that power looms will ruin the mill because machine-woven cloth is poorer than hers.
explanation: The introduction tells you Hannah is answering Cartwell's claim that the looms will free weavers. Her conditional ('If your engine weaves in a day what I weave in a week, then who will pay me...') and the 'But' sentence turn that claim around: the looms will take away weavers' livelihood rather than bring them relief.

B.why: This summarizes Cartwell's claim, which the introduction reports. Hannah mocks 'Free us, sir?' and rejects it, so this choice gets her position backward.

C.why: You took 'who will pay me for the other six days?' literally. Her point is that nobody will pay her. She is not asking about a payment plan, and the looms would not be the ones standing idle.

D.why: Hannah says nothing about the quality of machine-made cloth or about the mill failing. You added an argument the text never makes.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from an English translation of a nineteenth-century dialogue. A professor has just told his student Lena that regional dialects are corruptions of the standard language.
LENA: Corruptions, sir? Then was the standard never itself a dialect? Yet the speech of the capital was once a village tongue like any other, and it rose only because the court happened to sit there. If a dialect may become "correct" by the accident of where kings live, then correctness is a matter of power, not of grammar.
choices: Lena argues that the standard language owes its status to political circumstance, not superior grammar.
Lena agrees that regional dialects are flawed versions of a standard language that is more correct.
Lena asks the professor whether the language of the capital was ever regarded as a regional dialect.
Lena argues that schools should teach regional dialects in place of the standard form of the language.
explanation: Lena's conditional holds her claim: if a dialect becomes 'correct' because the court happened to sit in its region, then correctness comes from power rather than grammar. Her history of the capital's 'village tongue' supports that conclusion, so the choice that says the standard's status is political states her point.

B.why: This is the professor's view, given in the introduction. Lena's whole reply argues against it.

C.why: 'Then was the standard never itself a dialect?' is rhetorical. Lena answers it herself in the next sentence, so she is not really asking the professor anything.

D.why: Lena questions where 'correctness' comes from, but she never proposes changing what schools teach. This choice goes beyond what she says.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set aboard a trawler in 1958. The captain, Ewan Muir, has dismissed a young biologist's worry about his catch by remarking that the sea is too big to empty.
DR. SORENSEN: So said the men who fished the old cod banks, Captain. The sea is wide, I grant you, but a shoal is not. Your nets go where the fish gather to spawn. If you take them before they breed, then it matters little how many miles of water lie beyond your boat.
choices: Sorensen argues that the ocean's size cannot protect a fish population that is caught before it breeds.
Sorensen accepts that the ocean is too vast for fishing to seriously reduce the number of its fish.
Sorensen recounts how fishermen on the old cod banks once boasted about the size of their catches.
Sorensen argues that commercial fishing should be stopped until all of the cod banks have recovered.
explanation: Sorensen grants a small concession ('The sea is wide, I grant you') and then moves to her real point with 'but a shoal is not.' Her conditional finishes the argument: if fish are caught before they spawn, the size of the ocean makes no difference. The ocean's size does not protect a population fished at its spawning grounds.

B.why: This is the captain's remark from the introduction. Sorensen grants only that the sea is wide, then rejects his conclusion. You treated her concession as her claim.

C.why: The cod-bank fishermen come up in one clause, as a warning example that they once said what Muir says now. The text never mentions them boasting about catches, and the example is not her main point.

D.why: Sorensen warns about catching fish before they breed but never proposes stopping commercial fishing. This choice is a stronger claim than she makes.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set on a merchant ship in 1912. Captain Rourke has insisted that his crew is well fed, since the men have all the salted beef and ship's biscuit they want and none ever goes hungry.
DR. ABARA: Hunger is not the measure, Captain. A man may eat his fill each day and still sicken, if what he eats lacks what the body needs. Look at Hollis: his belly is full, yet his gums bleed and his old scars have opened. The body is starving long before the stomach complains.
choices: Dr. Abara argues that eating enough food does not ensure a person is getting the nourishment the body needs.
Dr. Abara agrees that the crew is healthy because the men have as much beef and biscuit as they want.
Dr. Abara argues that the salted beef itself is to blame for causing the illness that Hollis is suffering.
Dr. Abara notes that bleeding gums and reopened scars are the earliest signs that a sailor feels hungry.
explanation: The introduction gives you the captain's measure: nobody is hungry. Dr. Abara rejects that measure ('Hunger is not the measure'), and her conditional says a man can eat his fill and still get sick if his food lacks what the body needs. Hollis is her single example, and her last sentence sums up the argument: a full stomach is not proof of good nourishment.

B.why: This is Captain Rourke's position, taken from the introduction. Dr. Abara disputes it in her first sentence.

C.why: Dr. Abara says the diet lacks something the body needs, not that the beef actively causes harm. Blaming the beef goes further than her words support.

D.why: You focused on the Hollis detail and got it wrong. Dr. Abara says these symptoms appear even though he is not hungry, so they are not signs of hunger. She uses them to show his body is starving while his stomach is full.
